key_terms.meaning: Moulding sand that still holds 4-8% moisture and sets by clay bonding, used for most sand moulds
Ability of the rammed sand to let steam and gases escape through its pores; measured by the AFS permeability number
Ability of the sand to stay solid and not fuse at the pouring temperature of the metal
Pattern made in two halves, one for the cope and one for the drag, so the parting line can sit at mid-height
Cope and drag halves mounted on opposite faces of one plate and moulded together, giving perfect alignment
Pattern is made bigger than the part by s, where s ≈ 10 mm/m for cast iron and 20 mm/m for steel
Taper of 0.5° to 3° on vertical pattern faces so the pattern lifts out without tearing the sand
Extra 2-5 mm of metal left on faces that will be machined after casting
Moulding machine action that lifts the flask and table and drops it, packing sand by impact
Moulding machine action that presses a flat plate onto the sand to ram it from the top
The vertical passage that carries metal down from the pouring basin to the runner
The smallest cross-section in the gating system; it sets the flow rate for the whole system
System where the choke is at the ingates, so the runner stays full and the metal jets into the cavity
A reservoir of liquid metal, kept open to the cavity, that feeds shrinkage until the casting freezes
Casting modulus M = V/A, volume of the casting divided by its heat-losing surface area
Temperature gap between liquidus and solidus; pure metals have zero range, alloys a wide one
Degrees by which the poured metal is hotter than its liquidus temperature
Expendable wax pattern coated with ceramic slurry; the wax is melted out and metal poured into the fired shell
Defect where metal freezes before filling a thin or far section, leaving the corner incomplete
Crack formed while the casting is still hot, when shrinkage is blocked by a rigid mould or core

takeaways: Moulding sand must be strong enough to hold its shape, permeable enough to let gas out, and refractory enough to survive the pour; the three pull against each other and the mix is a compromise.
A pattern is the casting plus allowances - shrinkage, draft, machining, shake and distortion - so a wrong allowance gives a wrong part even with a perfect mould.
Pattern shape and moulding method are chosen together: complex parting lines need split or loose piece patterns, and large or heavy jobs move from bench to floor to pit.
In a gating system the choke sets the flow rate; a pressurized system keeps the runner full but jets, while a non-pressurized system fills smoothly and traps slag in a skim bob.
A riser works only if it stays liquid longer than the casting it feeds, which happens when the riser modulus is larger than the casting modulus.
Chvorinov's rule, t = k(V/A)², lets you compare freezing times of any two shapes without knowing the metal in detail; the shape with the larger volume-to-area ratio freezes last.
Freezing starts at the cold mould wall and moves inward; a narrow freezing range gives a skin and a columnar zone, a wide range gives a mushy zone that is hard to feed.
Melting must give the right composition and enough superheat; pouring must be smooth, central and fast enough to beat freezing but slow enough to avoid turbulence.
Shell, investment, die and centrifugal casting each trade mould cost against tolerance, surface finish and production rate; sand casting stays cheapest for large, one-off parts.
A defect's shape and position name its cause: rounded gas holes mean permeability or venting, ragged incomplete corners mean cold metal, cracks at a corner mean restrained shrinkage.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are marked on labelled sketches of the mould, pattern and gating system, on the definition-plus-reason style for each sand property and pattern allowance, and on numerical work with modulus or Chvorinov's rule.

bank.q: Draw a labelled section of a two-part sand mould and explain the function of each element, then list the properties a moulding sand must have.
outline: Sketch with cope, drag, parting line, sprue, pouring basin, runner, ingate, riser, core, mould cavity
Flask and sand support the cavity; parting line allows pattern removal
Gating carries metal in; riser feeds shrinkage; core makes the internal hole
Sand properties: green strength, dry strength, permeability, refractoriness, collapsibility, flowability, durability
Note the conflict: more clay raises strength but lowers permeability

bank.q: Explain the types of patterns used in foundries with a simple sketch of each, and state where each is used.
outline: Solid, split, match plate, cope-and-drag, loose piece, sweep, skeleton
Two lines on shape and the parting method for each
Sweep for large axisymmetric parts; skeleton for very large frames; loose piece for undercuts
Match plate for high production with alignment

bank.q: Define the five pattern allowances. Why is each needed, and how is its size decided?
outline: Shrinkage: metal contracts on cooling; about 10 mm/m cast iron, 20 mm/m steel
Machining: surface layer must be removed; 2-5 mm on machined faces only
Draft: taper for easy withdrawal; 0.5° to 3°
Shake or rapping: extra size because the pattern is rapped to loosen it
Distortion: added or removed metal to counter warping of U, V or long flat shapes
Reason for each, and that allowances are one-sided and additive in the right direction

bank.q: Describe bench, floor and pit moulding, and explain how a jolt-squeeze machine works.
outline: Bench: small moulds on a table, hand ramming
Floor: mould built on the foundry floor, medium and large jobs
Pit: mould sunk in a pit, very large castings, cope lifted by crane
Jolt: table lifted and dropped to ram sand by impact, best at the bottom
Squeeze: plate presses from the top, best at the top, hard and uniform
Jolt-squeeze combines both so the whole mould is evenly rammed

bank.q: Explain the elements of a gating system with a sketch and state the function of the pouring basin, sprue, runner, ingate and skim bob.
outline: Sketch with all elements in order
Pouring basin: receives metal, keeps slag back, provides head
Sprue: vertical drop; tapered downward to avoid air entrainment
Runner: distributes to ingates; skim bob traps slag
Ingate: controls entry into the cavity
Choke is the smallest area and controls the flow rate

bank.q: A plate casting has volume 1200 cm³ and total cooling surface area 900 cm². A riser is a cylinder of diameter equal to its height. Using Chvorinov's rule with n = 2, find the riser size so that it freezes 25% later than the casting.
outline: Compute casting modulus M = V/A = 1200/900 = 1.33 cm
Freezing time ratio (t_r/t_c) = (M_r/M_c)² = 1.25
For cylinder d = h: V = πd³/4, A = πd²/2 + πd²/4 = ... gives M = V/A = d/6
Hence d ≈ 8.9 cm, check the arithmetic
State that a real riser is made a little larger for safety

bank.q: Compare pressurized and non-pressurized gating systems and state which you would choose for (a) a tall steel casting and (b) an aluminium casting with a delicate sand core.
outline: Choke position: at ingates for pressurized, at sprue base for non-pressurized
Pressurized: runner full, small ingates, high velocity, more turbulence
Non-pressurized: larger downstream areas, slower entry, slag floats
Choice (a): non-pressurized or partly pressurized for smooth filling of steel
Choice (b): non-pressurized, low velocity protects the core, with a skim bob
Always design so the sprue does not draw air: taper the sprue

bank.q: For each case, suggest a casting process and give reasons: 100,000 small zinc alloy toy parts, a jet engine turbine blade in a nickel superalloy, a 2 m long cast iron water pipe, a 5-tonne machine tool bed.
outline: Zinc toys: hot chamber pressure die casting; high rate, good finish, low melting point
Turbine blade: investment casting; exact shape, superalloy, little machining
Water pipe: centrifugal casting; dense wall, no core, uniform thickness
Machine tool bed: sand casting in a pit; huge size, small batch, cheap
Each choice justified by tolerance, batch size, melting point and size

bank.q: A steel casting shows a large open cavity at the top of the heaviest section. Explain why it formed and how you would redesign the mould, using the idea of directional solidification.
outline: The heaviest section has the largest modulus, so it freezes last
No feed reaches it, so the last liquid leaves a shrinkage cavity
Place a riser on or beside that section, with riser modulus about 1.2 times the casting modulus
Feed the riser to the hot spot; use chills or padding so thinner parts freeze first
Keep a temperature gradient rising toward the riser
Feed the section through a short neck so the neck freezes after the casting

bank.q: Classify the common casting defects and, for any four, show how the shape and location of the defect points to its cause and remedy.
outline: Group by cause: sand, pattern, gating, pouring, solidification
Blowholes: round, inside, from gas; remedy: raise permeability, vent, lower moisture
Misrun and cold shut: incomplete thin sections, cold metal; raise pouring temperature, widen ingates
Sand inclusion and scab: ragged foreign material; better ramming, clean gating
Hot tear: crack at a restrained corner; collapsible core, fillets, even sections
Shrinkage cavity: rough open or internal void at the hot spot; riser, chill, padding

bank.q: Compare sand casting, die casting and investment casting on tolerance, surface finish, tooling cost, production rate and suitable metals, and recommend one for an automotive rocker cover in aluminium.
outline: Sand: wide metals, cheap tooling, poor finish, slow, best for small batches and large parts
Die: non-ferrous only, high tooling cost, excellent finish and tolerance, very high rate
Investment: high accuracy and finish for any alloy, slow and expensive per part
Rocker cover: aluminium, complex thin walls, large volume
Recommend pressure die casting for volume, or sand casting if volume is low
Trade-off between tooling cost and per-part cost

bank.q: Explain solidification of a pure metal and of an alloy, and discuss how the freezing range affects the feeding of a riser.
outline: Pure metal: freezes at one temperature, a smooth wall-to-centre front
Alloy: freezes between liquidus and solidus, a mushy zone of dendrites
Structure zones: chill zone, columnar zone toward the heat flow, equiaxed centre
Narrow range: skin forms, short feeding channel, riser works well
Wide range: dendrites block the channel, feeding is difficult, dispersed microshrinkage
Consequences for riser size and for choosing a process

bank.q: A foundry gets cracks at the corners of a box-shaped casting and blowholes on the top face. Analyse both problems and propose a combined remedy that does not simply raise the pouring temperature.
outline: Cracks: hot tears from restrained contraction; sharp corners and a rigid mould make it worse
Remedy: fillets, uniform section, collapsible or hollow core, reduce ramming hardness near corners
Blowholes: gas from moisture not escaping upward; low permeability or missing vents
Remedy: vent the cope, dry or reduce moisture, control clay, place the ingate so metal does not trap gas
Why raising pouring temperature helps gas but worsens tearing and shrinkage

glossary.def: The refractory cavity, usually rammed sand, that gives liquid metal its shape and removes its heat.
The top half of a moulding flask.
The bottom half of a moulding flask, on which the pattern is first placed.
The surface that separates cope from drag and along which the pattern is withdrawn.
A separate sand shape set in the mould to form a hole or internal passage in the casting.
A reservoir of liquid metal connected to the cavity, supplying metal as the casting contracts on freezing.
A metal or graphite insert in the mould wall that draws heat away fast and speeds local freezing.
The distance a metal flows in a standard channel before it stops; it falls as superheat falls.
Total freezing time t = k(V/A)², where k is a mould-and-metal constant, V the volume and A the heat-losing area.
The ratio M = V/A of a casting or riser; larger M means slower freezing.
Taper given to the vertical faces of a pattern so it can be lifted out of the sand.
Compressive strength of moist moulding sand, measured on a standard rammed specimen.
The last, smallest opening through which metal enters the mould cavity from the runner.
A funnel-shaped cup at the top of the sprue that receives the ladle stream and helps slag to float.
A rough void left where the last metal to freeze had no liquid feed.
A smooth, round, gas-filled hole inside or on the surface of a casting.
Loose sand or scale trapped in the casting, giving a ragged foreign spot.
Design of mould and risers so that freezing progresses steadily toward the riser.
An AFS index of sand coarseness; a high number means fine sand, low permeability and a smoother surface.
The temperature of the melt above its liquidus, in °C, at the moment of pouring.
Casting in a thin, resin-bonded sand shell made over a heated metal pattern.
Casting in a spinning mould, where centrifugal force holds the metal against the wall.
A ragged crack formed during cooling when contraction is blocked by a rigid mould or core.
A vertical shaft furnace, charged with alternate layers of coke, metal and limestone, used for cast iron.
